newsitem.title: POLAND: PSL MOUNTS PRESSURE ON POLISH PM OVER FARM POLICY.
newsitem.headline: PSL MOUNTS PRESSURE ON POLISH PM OVER FARM POLICY.

text.p: Poland's co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL) mounted pressure on Monday on Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz to force him to adopt the group's farm policy demands just a month before general elections.
The PSL drafed a no-confidence motion against Cimoszewicz, an ex-communist, but its senior official said the party may still drop it if the cabinet meets the demands.

"We have collected enough signatures under our motion to hold a parliamentary no-confidence vote against the prime minister," Janusz Piechocinski, a deputy head of the PSL parliamentary caucus, told Reuters.

Last week, the PSL said it would propose a no-confidence vote in parliament against Cimoszewicz, member of the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), accusing him of a delay in granting farmers advances for the 1997 grain harvest.
The advances were criticised by Finance Minister Marek Belka as too costly for the state budget.
But Piechocinski made clear that if the cabinet approved the proposals at its session on Tuesday the Peasants could bury the no-confidence motion.
"For us, personal changes is not the most important issue.. It is important that right farm policies are implemented," he said.
The government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska told a news briefing that the advance payments for farmers were on the government's Tuesday agenda.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski, linked to the ex-communist party, brushed off the Peasants' plans to oust the prime minister as campaigning before the elections, due on September 21.
"How else can we treat it (the no-confidence motion) if not as a pre-elections game," presidential spokesman Antoni Styrczula told reporters.
Opinion polls showed that the Peasants' rating is on decline and the party badly trails the elections' favourites -- the ex-communists and the opposition Solidarity Election Action (AWS).
Styrczula said that even in the unlikely event of dismissing Cimoszewicz in the parliamentary vote, the president will allow the cabinet to continue works until the elections.

The no-confidence motion, which could be voted late in August, has little chance to succeed because the oppostion is against it and the Peasants do not have the simple majority required to push it through.
